subject: Biotechnology
title: Monoclonal Antibodies
description: A quick win: understand Monoclonal Antibodies.

hook.text: Monoclonal antibodies are guided missiles — proteins designed to find and bind one specific target in the body.

buildup.text: Köhler and Milstein fused immune cells with cancer cells in 1975 — creating immortal antibody factories.

discovery.text: Each hybridoma produces one antibody type endlessly — pure, specific, and identical in every batch.

twist.text: Early mouse antibodies triggered human immune rejection — humanization replaced mouse parts with human ones.

climax.text: Monoclonal antibodies now treat cancer, arthritis, and COVID — seven of the top ten drugs are antibodies.

punchline.text: One antibody, one target — precision medicine at its finest.

quiz.question: Why did early mouse monoclonal antibodies fail in humans?
options: They were too large to enter human cells
The human immune system recognized mouse proteins as foreign and rejected them
Mouse antibodies could not bind to human targets

details.summary: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibody molecules produced from a single B cell clone, designed to bind one specific target with high precision. They are the largest class of biologic drugs, treating cancer, autoimmune diseases, and infections.
details.whyItMatters: Monoclonal antibodies represent over half of the best-selling drugs globally, generating over 200 billion dollars annually. Their precision targeting transformed treatment of cancers and autoimmune diseases that were previously difficult to treat.
takeaways: Monoclonal antibodies are identical molecules targeting one specific antigen
They are the largest class of biologic drugs by revenue globally
Applications span cancer therapy, autoimmune treatment, and infectious disease

faq.question: How are monoclonal antibodies produced for medical use?
faq.answer: Traditionally, mouse B cells producing desired antibodies are fused with immortal myeloma cells to create hybridomas. Modern methods use phage display or transgenic mice with human antibody genes. Production scales up in mammalian cell bioreactors.

faq.question: What diseases are treated with monoclonal antibodies?
faq.answer: Cancers including breast, lung, and blood cancers. Autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease. Inflammatory conditions like psoriasis. Infectious diseases including COVID-19. Migraine prevention and cholesterol reduction also use monoclonal antibodies.
